Applicant must hold unlimited out-of-state license issued upon completion of approved medical school and equivalent exam, hold unrestricted license for at least 4 years, have no disciplinary history, and have completed at least 1-2 years postgraduate training or hold ABMS specialty board certification.

Applicant must be licensed, certified, registered, or otherwise legally authorized to practice medicine in another U.S. state or approved jurisdiction; Board may waive the professional examination requirement.

Must meet requirements of the MOBILE Act (s. 456.0145): active unencumbered out-of-state license, national exam/certification or substantially similar requirements, 2 years of active practice in preceding 4 years, no pending disciplinary proceedings, no adverse disciplinary action in last 5 years, financial responsibility, fingerprints. Applicant must hold a current, unencumbered, active license in a jurisdiction with substantially equivalent or greater qualifications, have actively practiced medicine in another jurisdiction for at least two of the immediate preceding five years, and have no disciplinary actions or adverse patterns of negligence or incompetence.

Must comply with minimum requirements (degree, postgraduate training, character); must have passed an equivalent examination in another state/territory/Canada or by a recognized certifying agency approved by the board.

Applicant must hold a valid current license in another state/jurisdiction for at least one year; board waives examination, educational, or experience requirements if the other jurisdiction had minimum education requirements and verified the person met them. Applicant must not have had license revoked, not be under investigation or disciplinary action, must hold license in good standing, must not have a disqualifying criminal record.

A doctor of medicine may prescribe, dispense, administer, and furnish prescription drugs and devices, including controlled substances, subject to registration requirements and restrictions on schedule II opioids.
May prescribe, dispense, and administer drugs including controlled substances; may prescribe for pain including intractable pain; limited for substance use disorder treatment except as specified

Physicians and physician assistants may prescribe, dispense, and administer drugs including controlled substances in the course of legitimate professional practice, subject to limitations on opioid prescribing and electronic prescribing requirements.

Licensed physicians may prescribe drugs including controlled substances; must write prescriptions in English when requested; opioid prescriptions for first-time adult outpatient use limited to 7-day supply; for minors limited to 5-day supply

Physicians may prescribe, order, give, or administer drugs or medicine; all prescriptions must be electronic except in specified exceptions; prescriptions for dangerous or narcotic drugs must be for therapeutic or diagnostic purposes only.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, dispense, and administer legend drugs including controlled substances in Schedules II-V in the course of professional practice; may prescribe Schedule II-V controlled substances for treatment of intractable pain; opioid prescriptions for acute pain generally limited to 3-day supply (up to 7 days with documented justification). DEA registrants must complete CE on controlled substance prescribing.

Physicians licensed under this article may prescribe drugs and controlled substances; may delegate authority to prescribe/order to physician assistants and advanced practice registered nurses under job description or nurse protocol agreements; may issue controlled substance prescriptions within DEA and state regulations.

Physicians may use drugs and medicines as part of the practice of medicine, including prescribing; telehealth prescribing is held to the same standards as traditional settings; prescribing opiates or certifying cannabis use requires an in-person consultation.
Licensed physicians may prescribe, prescribe and furnish, and dispense prescription drugs and controlled substances incident to the practice of medicine.

Physicians may prescribe drugs including controlled substances; may not prescribe controlled substances via virtual care without compliance with 21 U.S.C. Prescribing narcotic or hallucinogenic drugs to maintain addiction or for other than treatment of disease is a disciplinary ground.
Any person licensed under this Act to practice medicine in all of its branches is authorized to purchase legend drugs and to dispense such legend drugs in the regular course of practicing medicine.
Licensed physicians may prescribe, direct, order, or designate the use of drugs and medicines in accordance with IC 25-1-9.3; subject to rules on controlled substances and opioid prescribing.

Physicians licensed to practice medicine and surgery may prescribe and dispense drugs, including controlled substances for medically accepted purposes. A special permit holder may prescribe drugs but not controlled substances.

Physicians may prescribe and administer drugs as part of the broad practice of medicine. Prescribing via telehealth requires proper physician-patient relationship establishment including verified identity, documented diagnosis, and maintained records.

Physicians may prescribe, dispense, and administer drugs including controlled dangerous substances; telehealth prescribing of controlled substances requires prior in-person examination except for patients in licensed healthcare facilities with DEA registration
Physicians may prescribe; telehealth prescribing authorized; medical students may not prescribe or dispense narcotic drugs.

Licensed physicians may prescribe drugs as part of medical practice; dispensing requires a permit under § 12-102 except for certain topical medications. Opioid prescribing is subject to statutory limits under § 1-223.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, administer, and dispense drugs including controlled substances for accepted therapeutic purposes. Prescribing opioid medication is subject to limits set in section 3300-F (100 MME/day cap with exceptions for cancer, palliative care, hospice, MAT, and certain institutional settings).

Licensed physicians may prescribe drugs including controlled substances in schedules 2-5. Physician's assistants may also prescribe drugs including controlled substances in schedules 2-5 under a practice agreement.
Licensed physicians may prescribe, give, or administer any drug or medicine for the use of another.

Physicians may prescribe, administer, and dispense drugs, including controlled substances. May prescribe controlled substances for therapeutic purposes for intractable pain. Prescriptions via telemedicine require establishment of a valid physician-patient relationship.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, recommend, or direct the use of drugs and medicines as part of the practice of medicine. Telemedicine prescribing requires a license from the State Board of Medical Licensure. Temporary license holders in drug/alcohol treatment programs may not apply for DEA controlled substances registration.

Physicians may prescribe drugs within their scope of practice; may dispense drugs if registered with the board of pharmacy and complying with applicable requirements. May not dispense controlled substances unless engaged in the practice of pharmacy.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, order, give, or administer any drug or medicine; may prescribe opioid antagonists directly or by standing order; drug prescribing authority may be delegated to physician assistants and nurse practitioners under supervision.

Physicians may prescribe, administer, and dispense drugs including controlled substances. Telemedicine prescribing of opioids is limited to FDA-approved medication assisted treatment for opioid use disorder or patients in hospital/long-term care. Prescribers of controlled substances must register with and comply with the North Dakota prescription drug monitoring program.

Physicians licensed under the Medicine and Surgery Practice Act may prescribe and furnish medicine; osteopathic physicians who have demonstrated adequate training may prescribe and administer drugs and medicines with board authorization.

Physicians may prescribe drugs including controlled substances (Schedule II-IV) via telemedicine and in-person; may prescribe for off-label indications under certain conditions; may not prescribe controlled substances without a valid physician-patient relationship.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, administer, and dispense drugs and controlled dangerous substances, subject to DEA registration requirements and state limitations on quantities (e.g., Schedule II CDS up to 30-day supply; or multiple prescriptions for up to 90-day supply under specified conditions). Physicians must access the Prescription Monitoring Program before prescribing certain controlled substances.

Licensed physicians may administer, dispense or prescribe drugs or medicine. Prescribing, administering or dispensing narcotic, stimulant or hypnotic drugs for other than accepted therapeutic purposes is unprofessional conduct.

Physicians are authorized to prescribe, administer, and dispense controlled substances and dangerous drugs as authorized by law. Prescribing controlled substances for intractable pain in accordance with NRS 639.23507 is not grounds for discipline. Physicians may also prescribe investigational drugs/biological products to terminally ill or life-threatened patients under specified conditions.

Licensed physicians may prescribe; statute explicitly authorizes prescribing non-patient-specific regimens to nurses (for immunizations, emergency treatment, various tests), and patient-specific or non-patient-specific orders to pharmacists (for immunizations, HIV PEP, insulin, hormonal contraceptives).

Physicians licensed to practice medicine and surgery or osteopathic medicine and surgery may prescribe, personally furnish, administer, and dispense drugs including controlled substances, subject to applicable state and federal rules. Physicians may also prescribe opioid analgesics and benzodiazepines subject to drug database check requirements.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, order, give, or administer any drug or medicine; prescribing controlled substances is subject to unprofessional conduct limits including opioid prescribing limits under 63 O.S. §2-309I

Licensed physicians may prescribe, administer, and dispense prescription drugs and controlled substances. Physicians may prescribe or administer controlled substances to patients in the course of treating diagnosed conditions causing pain.
Medical doctors may prescribe and administer drugs as part of the practice of medicine and surgery; clinical clerks may not prescribe or dispense drugs.

Licensed physicians may prescribe drugs; every prescription slip must contain the clearly-printed name and address of the issuing physician. Physicians must authorize generic substitution unless brand name is medically necessary. Physicians may not sign prescriptions in blank.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, order, give, or administer drugs or medicine. Prescribing requires establishment of a proper physician-patient relationship. Telemedicine prescribing of Schedule II-narcotic and Schedule III-narcotic controlled substances is restricted except in specified circumstances. Prescribing abortion-inducing drugs via telemedicine is prohibited.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, recommend, and direct the use of drugs and medicines; may prescribe and dispense Mifepristone and Misoprostol for medical abortions consistent with statutory requirements.
Licensed physicians may prescribe, dispense, and administer drugs, including controlled substances, in the course of professional practice.

A physician licensed under this subtitle may supply a patient with any drug, remedy, or clinical supply necessary to meet the patient's immediate needs. Physicians may prescribe dangerous drugs and controlled substances (with limitations), delegate prescribing to APRNs and PAs under prescriptive authority agreements, and dispense dangerous drugs in certain rural areas.

Licensed physicians may prescribe and administer drugs, including controlled substances, and may dispense drugs in licensed dispensing practices under specified conditions; opiate antagonists may be prescribed or dispensed without constituting unlawful or unprofessional conduct.

Physicians licensed to practice medicine or osteopathy may administer, prescribe, and dispense controlled substances to patients in a bona fide medical emergency or when pharmaceutical services are not available; also may prescribe dosages of pain-relieving agents in excess of recommended dosages upon certifying medical necessity.
Physicians may prescribe, order, give, and administer drugs and medicines; controlled substances are subject to restrictions including prohibition on self-prescribing.
Licensed physicians may administer and prescribe drugs or medicinal preparations; opioid prescribing rules must be adopted by the commission.

Physicians may prescribe drugs as part of the practice of medicine and surgery. They may prescribe opioid antagonists, antimicrobial drugs under expedited partner therapy, and other medications. Violation of ch. 450 (pharmacy) or 961 (controlled substances) constitutes unprofessional conduct.

Licensed physicians may prescribe, dispense, and administer drugs including controlled substances in good faith and for therapeutic purposes; telemedicine prescribing of Schedule II controlled substances is restricted (may not prescribe Schedule II to patients seen solely via telemedicine, except for established patients or specific exceptions).

Physicians may prescribe, order, give or administer drugs which can only be obtained by prescription. The board has authority over controlled substance prescribing, including requirements for prescribing via Internet.

Foreign medical graduates must be graduates of a medical school listed in the International Medical Education Directory or its equivalent, must pass each component of USMLE or COMLEX-USA within three attempts, and must complete ACGME- or AOA-approved graduate medical education.

Foreign medical graduates must have their medical school approved by the Arkansas State Medical Board and must additionally: (1) serve 3 years as intern/resident/fellow in accredited postgraduate program in the US; OR (2) serve 3 years in postgraduate program outside US, complete all USMLE steps, obtain ECFMG certification, and complete 1+ year ACGME-accredited fellowship or receive ABMS certification; OR (3) complete 1 year in accredited postgraduate program in US and be enrolled in accredited postgraduate program in Arkansas. For temporary license in critical shortage areas, foreign graduate

Foreign medical graduates must obtain ECFMG certification, complete 24 months of board-approved postgraduate training (vs. 12 months for US/Canada graduates), and have their medical school recognized by the board. ECFMG certification status must be submitted directly to the board.

International medical graduates must complete one year of postgraduate clinical training approved by the board. If the medical school is not an approved medical college, the applicant may still be eligible at board discretion if they hold current specialty board certification from ABMS or AOA.

Foreign medical graduates must have received the degree of doctor of medicine, osteopathic medicine or its equivalent, satisfy educational requirements specified in regulations, and either (i) successfully completed all components of a 'fifth pathway program' conducted by an American medical school accredited by AMA or AOA, or (ii) received certification from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG).

Foreign medical graduates from schools listed in IMED must pass the ECFMG examination and the Federation of State Medical Boards examination. Graduates from schools not listed in IMED must also complete 3 years of postgraduate training in an ACGME-approved residency program. All foreign graduates must provide documentary proof that U.S./Canadian clinical rotations were in accredited institutions.

Foreign medical graduates must either: (1) graduate from a WHO-registered foreign medical school certified under s. 458.314 as meeting US accreditation standards, pass an English proficiency requirement if not taught in English, and complete at least 1 year of approved residency; or (2) graduate from an uncertified foreign medical school, obtain ECFMG evaluation and certificate, pass ECFMG exam, and complete at least 2 years of approved residency or fellowship after October 1, 1992. Graduates of non-board-approved foreign medical schools who graduated after July 1, 1985 must complete three years of ACGME/AOA/board-approved residency, fellowship, or postgraduate training. Foreign medical graduates must also generally reside in the US for one year prior to examination (except Canadian graduates). ECFMG certification pathway available for students completing supervised clinical training.

Foreign medical school graduates must have at least two years of residency in an ACGME- or AOA-accredited program (or Canadian equivalent), and must hold the ECFMG national certificate (or pass the Medical Council of Canada Evaluating Examination for Canadian residency), or hold the Fifth Pathway Program certificate of the AMA.

Foreign medical graduates must present a valid standard certificate issued by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or similar accrediting agency, and must provide satisfactory evidence of successful completion of two years of postgraduate internship or resident training (vs. one year for domestic graduates).

International physicians must be graduates of an international medical program evaluated and certified by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG), must pass USMLE steps 1 and 2, must have completed post-graduate medical training, must have practiced medicine in good standing for at least 3 years or completed 500 hours of supervised clinical experience in the US, must have an offer of employment at a sponsoring entity in Idaho with a supervising physician, and receive a 3-year provisional license before applying for a full license.

International medical graduates must have education certified by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG), passed USMLE Steps 1, 2 CK, and 3, maintain an unencumbered license from another country, and not be licensed in any U.S. state or territory. After January 1, 2025, IMGs may apply for a limited license with a pathway to full licensure after a supervision period.

Foreign medical graduates must complete a minimum of two years of postgraduate training in a US or Canadian hospital approved by nationally recognized medical accrediting bodies (board may waive second year). Foreign medical graduates must pass an examination given by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) in addition to other required examinations. For a postgraduate permit, a foreign medical school graduate must also have passed the ECFMG examination.

Graduates of medical schools outside the United States or Canada must: speak/read/write English; complete prerequisite coursework; graduate from a board-approved foreign medical school (or be a US citizen with a diploma from a US school obtained via transfer program); pass the board-prescribed examination; be certified by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or an approved US specialty board; complete a postgraduate training program of duration established by the board.

International medical graduates must hold a medical doctorate or substantially similar degree from an international medical program of good standing, be in good standing with the medical licensing institution of their country, have completed a residency or practiced as a physician for at least 5 years in their licensing country, be a U.S. or Canadian citizen or legally entitled to live and work in the U.S. with basic English fluency, and have an offer of employment at a licensed hospital facility in Louisiana. They must provide medical services only at a facility owned or operated by a license

Special pathway exists for internationally-trained physicians via limited license program requiring USMLE Steps 1, 2-CK, and 3 and participation in a qualifying healthcare facility program.

Foreign medical graduates must be certified by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG), pass a qualifying examination for foreign medical graduates required by the Board, and complete either 2 years of postgraduate training in an accredited program or complete a fifth pathway program plus 2 years of postgraduate training.

Foreign medical graduates from unaccredited schools must either obtain ECFMG permanent certificate or pass the Visa Qualifying Examination (or equivalent). For postgraduate training, 36 months in ACGME-accredited program required. A waiver is available for foreign graduates who are licensed in another state and have 3+ years of clinical experience, upon board review.

Foreign medical graduates applying for a full license must demonstrate: 10+ years of practice after completing their medical degree; completion of not less than 3 years of postgraduate clinical training at an institution affiliated with a WHO-listed medical school approved by the board; a passing score on a board-approved initial medical licensure examination; and safe/competent practice under a clinical academic limited license in Michigan for at least 2 years immediately preceding application (at least 800 hours/year). Graduates of foreign medical schools must be recognized by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates; board members include those recognized by ECFMG. The IMLC defines eligible physicians as graduates of medical schools listed in the International Medical Education Directory.

Foreign medical graduates may receive a limited institutional license for practice in Mississippi state institutions. License is limited to a particular institution, valid for one year, renewable annuall
Graduates of foreign medical schools outside the US and Canada must pass an examination offered by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or its successors.

Graduates of international medical schools must have: a currently valid ECFMG certificate, ability to communicate in English, good moral character, two years of postgraduate training in a Board-approved program (or proof of current specialty board certification), and must pass each part of an examination described in G.S. 90-10.1.

International medical school graduates must: (1) possess degree of doctor of medicine or board-approved equivalent; (2) complete 24 months of postgraduate training in a US/Canadian accredited program (or at least 12 months if equivalent experience found); (3) present ECFMG certificate; (4) demonstrate working ability in English. Osteopathic graduates from outside the US are not eligible.

Foreign medical graduates must provide a copy of a permanent certificate issued by the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) currently effective, or credentials certifying they have passed the Visa Qualifying Examination or its successor required by DHHS and USCIS; and must serve at least two years (rather than one) of board-approved graduate medical education.

Graduates of foreign medical schools must have studied at a school recognized by the United Nations World Health Organization (UNWHO) and have studies confirmed by Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) Certification. Foreign medical graduates who graduated prior to January 1, 1970 need only 12 months of approved postgraduate training.

Graduates of foreign medical schools must present a diploma from a legally incorporated professional school or college of a foreign country that was in good standing in the board's opinion, prove four full school years of study, and meet all postgraduate training requirements. For IMLC expedited licensure, the physician must be a graduate of a medical school listed in the International Medical Education Directory or its equivalent.

A graduate of a board-approved medical or osteopathic medical school located outside the United States or Canada must present evidence of good moral character, pass a board-required examination, and complete two years of postgraduate medical training in an approved program. A graduate of a medical school outside the U.S. who completed at least two years of an approved postgraduate training program at or affiliated with a New Mexico institution prior to December 30, 2007 may also be granted a license.

Foreign medical graduates must submit proof of degree of doctor of medicine or its equivalent as determined by the Board, and the standard certificate of the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or a written statement that the applicant passed the ECFMG examination. Proof of degree must be submitted directly by the foreign medical school.

A foreign physician must hold a standard certificate from the Educational Council for Foreign Medical Graduates or pass an exam satisfactory to the state board for medicine. Alternatively, a US resident enrolled in a foreign medical school recognized by the WHO may qualify if they complete formal requirements (except internship/social service), attain a satisfactory score on a qualifying examination accepted by an LCME-approved school, complete one academic year of supervised clinical training, complete required post-graduate hospital training, and pass the licensing examination.

Foreign medical graduates must hold certification from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) and complete at least 24 months of graduate medical education through the second-year level. Foreign applicants must possess the degree of Doctor of Medicine or a Board-approved equivalent evidenced by ECFMG; must demonstrate English language proficiency satisfactory to the Board as determined by ECFMG; must provide ECFMG Certificate or Medical Council of Canada Certificate of Registration; Board may require 12–24 months of Board-approved progressive graduate medical training; must meet immigration status requirements.

Graduates of unaccredited medical colleges must complete two years of approved graduate medical training, meet educational requirements prescribed by the board, and obtain certification by the Educational Council for Foreign Medical Graduates (ECFMG) or its successors.

Internationally trained physicians must have ECFMG certification, completed residency in ACGME-I or WFME-recognized program, and been licensed in another country for at least 3 years. If the diploma is from a medical or osteopathic college outside the United States, the Board of Examiners may require further proof of competence by rules adopted pursuant to chapter 1-26.

International medical school graduates must submit a permanent ECFMG certificate, a certificate from a medical school whose curriculum is acceptable to the board, and evidence of satisfactory completion of a three-year post-graduate training program approved by the AMA. Foreign medical graduates must submit current ECFMG certification (or qualify under the fifth pathway program which requires passing ECFMG or USMLE Parts I and II, one year of supervised clinical training in a US accredited program, and completion of postgraduate hospital training). Foreign teaching licenses are available for those with recognized foreign credentials invited by an LCME-accredited Utah medical school.

Foreign graduates must exhibit a diploma, license, or certificate conferring full right to practice in their country or satisfactory evidence of equivalent study and examinations. The Board may issue a nonrenewable temporary license (up to 2 years) for advanced training in an approved institute, or a provisional license (up to 2 years) to foreign graduates with at least 5 years of practice, ECFMG certification, passing scores on USMLE Steps 1 and 2 CK, and an agreement with a medical care facility for an assessment program.

Graduates of medical schools outside the U.S. or Canada must complete at least three years (vs. two for U.S./Canadian graduates) of postgraduate training in an accredited U.S. or Canadian program and must submit ECFMG certification unless qualifying as a Fifth Pathway applicant.

Foreign medical graduates must: complete a course of professional instruction equivalent to that required generally; satisfy ECFMG certification; demonstrate English language ability; meet all other standard requirements. An exceptional qualification waiver is available. For limited licenses, ECFMG certification and passage of USMLE steps 1 and 2 are required.

Foreign medical graduates must: (1) hold a diploma from a foreign medical college credentialed by a board-approved agency; (2) obtain ECFMG certification; (3) pass all steps of the USMLE; and (4) complete 24 months of ACGME- or AOA-accredited postgraduate training. A provisional license is available for international physicians with certain employer sponsorship, 5 years' practice experience post-residency, and USMLE passage.

Foreign medical graduates must hold a valid ECFMG certificate (or meet specified alternative requirements), complete a minimum of two years of ACGME-approved graduate clinical training (or one year plus ABMS board certification, or two years of fellowship), and demonstrate ability to communicate in English.

Foreign medical graduates must obtain ECFMG certification as an alternative to LCME or AOA accredited school graduation. The 'Fifth pathway' program is available for students who studied at a foreign medical school, completed all formal requirements except internship, passed specified examinations, and completed an LCME-supervised academic year of clinical education.

fields.rationale: States cluster around: explicit day-supply caps on opioid prescriptions, MME/dose-based caps, restrictions specific to telehealth prescribing, delegation of limit-setting to board rulemaking, and states relying purely on disciplinary grounds without numeric limits — with a small group focused on stimulants/Schedule II rather than opioids specifically.

assignments.raw_value: Initial opioid prescription to an adult may not exceed a seven-day supply; all opioid prescriptions for minors may not exceed a seven-day supply. Exceptions apply for acute medical conditions, chronic pain, cancer, palliative care, logistical/travel barriers, or substance abuse treatment.

Excessive prescribing of Schedule II controlled substances is a disciplinary ground. Schedule II amphetamines and stimulants may only be prescribed for specific therapeutic indications (narcolepsy, hyperkinesis, specific brain dysfunction, epilepsy, clinically significant depression refractory to other treatment); treatment for depression-related indications shall not extend beyond 30 days unless patient is referred to a specialist.

The Arkansas State Medical Board is authorized to promulgate rules limiting the amount of Schedule II narcotics that may be prescribed and dispensed by licensees. A physician shall not be subject to disciplinary action solely for prescribing dangerous or controlled drugs for relief of chronic intractable pain when within appropriate criteria.

A doctor of medicine may not dispense a schedule II controlled substance that is an opioid, except for an implantable device or an opioid that is for medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorders. Dispensing a schedule II controlled substance that is an opioid is unprofessional conduct except as provided in sections 32-1491 and 32-3248.03.

No specific quantity/duration limits stated in the statute, but excessive prescribing of controlled substances without good faith prior examination is grounds for discipline. Prescribing for intractable pain consistent with lawful prescribing is protected.

A prescriber shall not prescribe more than a seven-day supply of an opioid to a new patient (one who has not obtained an opioid prescription from that prescriber within the last twelve months), with an option for a second seven-day supply fill. Exceptions apply for chronic pain, cancer pain, post-surgical pain expected to exceed fourteen days, and palliative/hospice care.

When issuing a first prescription for an opioid drug to an adult patient for outpatient use, a prescribing practitioner may not prescribe more than a 7-day supply. For minors, no more than a 5-day supply. Exceptions exist for acute medical conditions requiring more, chronic pain, cancer-related pain, and palliative care.

For acute pain, opioid prescriptions (Schedule II) may not exceed a 3-day supply; up to 7-day supply may be prescribed if clinically justified and documented with 'ACUTE PAIN EXCEPTION' noted. For non-acute pain, prescriber must indicate 'NONACUTE PAIN' on Schedule II opioid prescriptions. For traumatic injuries with ISS ≥9, concurrent prescription of emergency opioid antagonist required.

No general statutory opioid prescribing limits for physicians. Board authorized to establish minimum standards for prescribing controlled substances for pain management. Schedule II opioids (hydrocodone, oxycodone) may be delegated to PAs and APRNs only in emergency situations with a 5-day supply maximum.
For purposes of prescribing opiates via telehealth, a physician-patient relationship shall only be established after an in-person consultation between the prescribing physician and the patient.

The board of medicine must adopt rules establishing penalties for prescribing practitioners that prescribe opioids in dosage amounts exceeding what would be prescribed by a reasonably prudent prescribing practitioner engaged in the same practice.

The medical licensing board shall adopt rules establishing standards and protocols for prescribing controlled substances; rules on conditions exempted from opioid prescription limitations under IC 25-1-9.7-2; rules on appropriate prescribing of Schedule III or IV controlled substances for weight reduction or obesity; and board must adopt rules on conditions exempt from prescribing limitations set forth in IC 25-1-9.7-2(a).

Licensees may prescribe amphetamines and sympathomimetic amines designated in Schedule II, III, or IV only for specified medical purposes including narcolepsy, drug-induced brain dysfunction, ADHD, depression, obesity, binge eating disorder, and other board-approved conditions. Prescribing for other than lawful or medically accepted purposes is a disciplinary ground.

On treatment for pain, a health care provider shall prescribe the lowest effective dose of an opioid and a quantity no greater than needed for the expected duration of pain, unless treating substance-related disorder, cancer pain, end-of-life/hospice/palliative care, or chronic pain. Dosage must follow evidence-based clinical guidelines.

May not prescribe opioids in excess of 100 morphine milligram equivalents per day; no more than 30-day supply for chronic pain within a 30-day period; no more than 7-day supply for acute pain within 7-day period (with certain exceptions for cancer, palliative/hospice care, MAT, and institutional/surgical settings).

Physicians may prescribe controlled substances for therapeutic purposes for intractable pain. No specific statutory limit on quantity or duration for opioids is set out in the statute beyond general therapeutic purpose requirements. Ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine prescribing is explicitly protected from discipline.

When prescribing opioids to opioid-naive patients on an outpatient basis, the prescription may not be for more than a 7-day supply, except for chronic pain, cancer-related pain, palliative care, or opioid abuse/dependence treatment. This provision is temporary and terminates June 30, 2025.

Opioids may only be prescribed through telemedicine if prescribed as FDA-approved medication assisted treatment for opioid use disorder or to a patient in a hospital or long-term care facility; opioids may not be prescribed through telemedicine for any other purpose.

Initial opioid prescriptions are limited to a 5-day supply under P.L.2017, c.28. Schedule II CDS generally limited to 30-day supply per prescription; multiple prescriptions may be issued for up to 90-day total supply under specified conditions. Schedule II CDS may only be prescribed via telemedicine after an initial in-person examination, with subsequent in-person visits required every three months.

Physicians must check the state drug database before prescribing opioid analgesics or benzodiazepines, and must recheck at least every 90 days during ongoing treatment. Exceptions apply for prescriptions not exceeding 7 days, cancer treatment, hospice patients, terminally ill patients, hospital/nursing home administration, and post-surgical acute pain. Separate rules apply for prescribing opioids to minors.
Prescribing opioid drugs in excess of the maximum limits authorized in Section 2-309I of Title 63 of the Oklahoma Statutes constitutes unprofessional conduct

Via telemedicine, Schedule II-narcotic and Schedule III-narcotic prescriptions are not permitted except when: the patient is physically located in a hospital being treated by a practitioner; for patients actively enrolled in a Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) program with buprenorphine for opioid use disorder; patients enrolled in palliative care or hospice; or other programs specifically authorized by the board. Physician assistants may prescribe Schedule II controlled substances (oral) for no more than an initial 5-day supply, with subsequent prescriptions requiring supervising physician

A physician may delegate the prescribing or ordering of a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV, or V only if the prescription (including refills) is for a period not to exceed 90 days. Delegation of Schedule II prescribing is limited to hospital facility-based practice or hospice care. Physicians must follow board guidelines for opioid antagonist prescribing.

The Board shall adopt regulations for prescribing opioids including requirements for patient history and evaluation, limitations on dosages or day supply of drugs for acute pain, documentation requirements, and mandatory use of the Prescription Monitoring Program. Chronic pain treatment must include a treatment plan, signed patient agreement, and periodic review.

By January 1, 2019, the commission must adopt rules establishing requirements for prescribing opioid drugs, which may include dosing criteria and exemptions. Specific numeric limits are set by rule, not statute.

A physician practicing solely via telemedicine may not prescribe Schedule II controlled substances except to established patients or members of the same group practice. A physician may not prescribe Schedule II pain-relieving controlled substances for chronic nonmalignant pain solely based on a telemedicine encounter (except for established patients).

Statute prohibits initially prescribing any controlled substance via the Internet, World Wide Web or similar electronic system absent a documented physician-patient relationship. Repeated prescribing of scheduled drugs to a known abuser or to family members or self is a disciplinary ground.

fields.rationale: States cluster around six dominant approaches: asserting parity with in-person care, requiring an established provider-patient relationship, imposing specific controlled-substance prescribing limits, requiring an in-person exam before prescribing, clarifying licensure/jurisdictional scope, or delegating details to board rulemaking — each bucket reflects the primary thrust of the statutory text even though many states touch multiple themes.

assignments.raw_value: The board may not impose disciplinary sanctions on a physician for prescribing non-controlled substances via telehealth if follow-up care is available and records are offered to the primary care provider. Controlled substances may be prescribed via telehealth if those requirements and opioid limits are met. Physicians may not prescribe in response to an Internet questionnaire or email without a prior physician-patient relationship.

A prescriber may prescribe legend drugs or controlled substances as a result of telehealth if authorized under state and federal law. Controlled substance prescriptions via telehealth require: (1) synchronous audio or audio-visual HIPAA-compliant communication, (2) at least one in-person encounter with the patient in the preceding 12 months, and (3) established legitimate medical purpose in the preceding 12 months. Exception for medical emergencies as defined by board rule.

Healthcare services provided by telemedicine, including a prescription through telemedicine, shall be held to the same standard of care as healthcare services provided in person. A professional relationship must be established before providing telemedicine services. A physician licensed in Arkansas who has access to a patient's personal health record may use telemedicine, including the telephone, with a patient located in Arkansas to diagnose, treat, and if clinically appropriate, prescribe a noncontrolled drug.

A physical or mental health status examination required before prescribing may be conducted through telehealth with a clinical evaluation appropriate for the patient and condition, except for written certification for medical marijuana purposes. Prescriptions written by a licensee through a telehealth program covered by hospital or outpatient treatment center policies and procedures are also exempt from the examination requirement.

An appropriate prior examination for prescribing dangerous drugs does not require a synchronous interaction and can be achieved through telehealth, including self-screening tools or questionnaires, provided the licensee complies with the appropriate standard of care.

Telemedicine is recognized as part of the practice of medicine. Physicians must practice within their scope and comply with generally accepted standards of medical practice when providing telemedicine services. Any act or omission in telemedicine that fails to meet generally accepted standards constitutes unprofessional conduct.

The provisions of the medical practice act apply to any individual whose practice of medicine includes any ongoing, regular or contractual arrangement providing diagnostic or treatment services through electronic communications to any person located in Connecticut. For radiographic images, licensure is required for out-of-state physicians providing official written reports of diagnostic evaluations through an ongoing, regular or contractual arrangement.

A physician located outside the State who renders a written or otherwise documented medical opinion concerning the diagnosis or treatment of a person, or who actually renders treatment to a person within the State as a result of transmission of the person's medical data by electronic or other means, is considered to be practicing medicine in Delaware.

Telehealth providers may not prescribe Schedule II controlled substances via telehealth unless for treatment of a psychiatric disorder, inpatient hospital treatment, hospice services, or nursing home residents. Telehealth providers must practice consistent with prevailing professional standard of care and may not perform abortions via telehealth.

Physicians practicing telemedicine in Georgia must hold a full Georgia license or a Georgia telemedicine license. The practice of medicine occurs where the patient is located. Telemedicine licensees are not authorized to engage in the practice of medicine while physically present in Georgia with a patient also physically present, except in emergencies.

Treatment recommendations via telehealth, including issuing prescriptions electronically, are held to the same standards as traditional physician-patient settings. Issuing a prescription based solely on an online questionnaire is not acceptable. For opiates or cannabis certification, an in-person consultation is required first.

A provider with an established provider-patient relationship may issue prescription drug orders via virtual care within the scope of the provider's license and applicable laws, but controlled substances may not be prescribed unless in compliance with 21 U.S.C. Treatment based solely on a static online questionnaire is not an acceptable standard of care.

A person who engages in the practice of telemedicine without a license or permit issued under this Act is subject to penalties. A person with a temporary permit for health care may treat a patient located in Illinois through telehealth services consistent with the person's scope of practice and agreement with a sponsoring entity.

The board may adopt rules under IC 4-22-2 establishing guidelines for the practice of telehealth in Indiana. Telehealth diagnostic or treatment services transmitted through electronic communications on a regular, routine, and nonepisodic basis or under an oral or written agreement constitute the practice of medicine. A nonresident physician outside Indiana does not practice medicine in Indiana by providing a second opinion or follow-up diagnostic/treatment services.

A physician practicing telemedicine under a telemedicine waiver shall conduct an appropriate assessment and evaluation of the patient's current condition and document the appropriate medical indication for any prescription issued.

A physician prescribing via telehealth (electronic/computer means) must establish a proper physician-patient relationship including: verification of patient identity, establishment of a documented diagnosis through accepted medical practices, and maintenance of a current medical record. An electronic, online, or telephonic evaluation by questionnaire is inadequate for initial or follow-up evaluation.

A physician practicing telemedicine shall not prescribe any controlled dangerous substance prior to conducting an appropriate in-person patient history or physical examination of the patient, except when the patient is being treated at a licensed healthcare facility with a current DEA registration, in which case the physician may prescribe any controlled dangerous substance without necessity of conducting an in-person examination.

Physicians licensed by the board may provide telehealth services including prescribing via synchronous or asynchronous audio, video, electronic media or telecommunications technology, and may obtain proxy credentialing and privileging for telehealth services with other health care providers or facilities complying with CMS conditions of participation.

A physician not licensed in Maine may provide consultative services through interstate telehealth if registered with the board every 2 years, fully licensed without restriction in their home state, not opening an office or meeting patients in Maine, and providing only consultative services at the request of a Maine-licensed practitioner who retains ultimate authority.

A health professional providing telehealth services may prescribe drugs, including controlled substances, if acting within the scope of practice and meeting applicable controlled substance prescribing requirements. Must provide referral for geographically accessible services if medically necessary, and must make follow-up care available.

A physician providing health care services by telehealth in this state shall be held to the same standards of practice and conduct as provided in this chapter for in-person health care services. A physician-patient relationship may be established through telehealth.

Prior to prescribing any drug or controlled substance through telemedicine or the internet, a physician must establish a valid physician-patient relationship, including obtaining a reliable medical history and performing a physical examination adequate to establish the diagnosis. Prescribing based solely on a telephone evaluation is prohibited unless a previously established and ongoing physician-patient relationship exists.

Telemedicine (practice of medicine across state lines) requires a full Mississippi medical license unless: the evaluation/treatment/opinion is requested by a Mississippi-licensed physician AND that physician has already established a doctor-patient relationship with the patient.

Telemedicine is included within the practice of medicine. Audio-only telemedicine for physicians providing written certification of a debilitating medical condition is not permitted unless a prior in-person physician-patient relationship exists. The board shall provide guidelines by administrative rule for the practice of telemedicine by physicians.

The practice of medicine includes performing acts by use of any electronic or other means, including the internet or telephone; nonregistered physicians in another state may treat their own regular patients temporarily in NC by any method of communication.

A licensee who has performed a telemedicine examination or evaluation meeting statutory requirements may prescribe medications according to professional discretion and judgment. Opioids may only be prescribed via telemedicine for FDA-approved medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder, or for patients in hospital or long-term care facilities. Controlled substance prescribers must participate in the ND prescription drug monitoring program.

Telehealth is authorized broadly; physicians located in another state who through any medium (including electronic) perform for compensation any service constituting the healing arts affecting diagnosis or treatment of an individual in Nebraska are deemed to be practicing medicine in Nebraska and must be licensed.

A physician may prescribe non-opioid and opioid controlled drugs classified in Schedule II through IV via telemedicine; a subsequent in-person or telehealth evaluation must occur at intervals appropriate for the patient but not less than annually. All prescribing must comply with federal and state laws. A valid physician-patient relationship is required, which may be established via telemedicine under certain conditions.

Prescriptions issued via telemedicine are held to the same standard of care as in-person settings. A provider shall not issue a prescription to a patient based solely on responses to an online static questionnaire unless a proper provider-patient relationship has been established. Schedule II CDS may only be prescribed via telemedicine after an initial in-person examination, and a subsequent in-person visit is required every three months for the duration. Exception: stimulant Schedule II CDS for minors under 18 may be prescribed via telemedicine using interactive real-time two-way audio/video

A telemedicine license allows a physician to practice medicine across state lines. The practice of medicine across state lines includes rendering written or documented medical opinions concerning diagnosis or treatment of a New Mexico patient by a physician outside the state, or rendering treatment to a New Mexico patient from outside the state, via electronic, telephonic or other transmission.

A physician located at a distant site may use telehealth to write treatment orders or prescriptions for patients in Nevada if the physician holds a valid Nevada license, including a special purpose license. The practice of medicine via telehealth is deemed to occur at the patient's location. The special purpose license allows out-of-state physicians to practice telemedicine in Nevada if they hold a full unrestricted license elsewhere, have had no disciplinary action, and are certified by a specialty board of the ABMS.

Physicians may provide telehealth services under standards established by the state medical board. For non-controlled substances, physicians may establish a physician-patient relationship through appropriate technology permitting medical evaluation consistent with minimal standard of care. For controlled substances, standards must be consistent with federal law. Boards may require an initial in-person visit before prescribing schedule II controlled substances to new patients except for hospice/palliative care, opioid use disorder treatment, mental health patients, or emergency situations.

Performance by a person outside this state through an ongoing regular arrangement of diagnostic or treatment services through electronic communications for a patient being diagnosed or treated within Oklahoma by a licensed Oklahoma physician constitutes practicing medicine and surgery in Oklahoma (and therefore requires licensure), but a physician with a valid Oklahoma license may perform such services

A physician licensed under ORS 677.100 to 677.228 may use telemedicine to engage in the practice of medicine and provide health care services, including the establishment of a provider-patient relationship, the diagnosis or treatment of a medical condition or the prescription of drugs, to a patient physically located in this state. The physician is not required to be physically located in this state when engaging in the practice of medicine through telemedicine.

A licensee practicing via telemedicine must prescribe in accordance with Section 40-47-113, participate in the South Carolina Prescription Monitoring Program, and comply with the Ryan Haight Act. Schedule II-narcotic and Schedule III-narcotic prescriptions are generally prohibited except for patients physically in a hospital, MAT program patients receiving buprenorphine, hospice/palliative care patients, or board-authorized programs. Prescribing abortion-inducing drugs is prohibited. At each encounter, a medical history interview must be conducted by the prescribing licensee. Establishing a ph

Any nonresident physician or osteopath who, while located outside this state, provides diagnostic or treatment services through electronic means to a patient located in this state is engaged in the practice of medicine or osteopathy in this state and is subject to South Dakota licensure requirements.

A physician may prescribe via telemedicine if a valid practitioner-patient relationship exists. This requires either a preexisting relationship, a call coverage arrangement, or synchronous audiovisual interaction or asynchronous store-and-forward with access to relevant clinical information. A practitioner-patient relationship is not present if prescribing an abortifacient or drug to terminate a pregnancy. Physicians must provide follow-up guidance and share records with the patient's primary care physician.

An out-of-state doctor of medicine or osteopathy who holds an active, unrestricted license in another state and has a previously established practitioner-patient relationship (with in-person examination within previous 12 months) may provide continuity of care via telemedicine services in the Commonwealth for up to one year per patient for behavioral health services, or for other care generally under an exemption from licensure.

Prescribing via electronic means requires reasonable efforts to verify patient identity, documented diagnosis through accepted medical practices, and maintenance of a current medical record; electronic questionnaire-only evaluation is inadequate for initial evaluation except for pregnancy termination medication.

Physicians practicing via telemedicine may not prescribe Schedule II controlled substances to patients seen solely through telemedicine, except for established patients or members of the same group practice, specific categories of minors with developmental disabilities, or hospital inpatient orders. Schedule II pain-relieving drugs for chronic nonmalignant pain may not be prescribed solely based on a telemedicine encounter (except established patients). Treatment based solely on an online questionnaire is not acceptable standard of care.

Statute prohibits initially prescribing any controlled substance through the Internet or similar electronic system absent a documented physician-patient relationship. The board has authority to adopt rules and regulations for the practice of telemedicine.

fields.rationale: States cluster primarily by which controlled substance schedules PAs may prescribe, whether Schedule II is fully included, restricted, or excluded, with a separate bucket for states where authority is entirely delegated by a supervising physician and another for states that defer scope entirely to board rules or collaborative agreements without specifying schedules.

assignments.raw_value: Physician assistants may prescribe, dispense, or administer prescription drugs (including controlled substances) under regulations adopted by the board governing their scope of activities, subject to the same telehealth and opioid prescribing limitations as physicians.

A licensed assistant to a physician registered to a licensed physician may prescribe legend drugs to patients, subject to: (1) drug type, dosage, quantity, and refills authorized in a board-approved job description signed by the supervising physician; and (2) the drug must be on the formulary approved under Board of Medical Examiners guidelines. Assistants may not prescribe controlled substances except as ordered by the physician in writing or by verbal order reduced to writing.

A supervising physician may delegate prescriptive authority to a graduate registered physician to include prescribing, ordering, and administering Schedules III-V controlled substances, all legend drugs, and all nonschedule prescription medications and medical devices. A graduate registered physician's level of prescriptive authority shall not exceed the authority of the supervising physician.

Physician assistants with a collaborative agreement may prescribe and dispense medication, including controlled substances, to the extent and in the manner authorized by board rules and within the physician assistant's education, experience, and competency.

A physician assistant may, as delegated by the supervising physician: prescribe and administer drugs including controlled substances in schedule IV or V in all settings; renew prescriptions for controlled substances in schedule II, III, IV or V in all settings; prescribe and administer controlled substances in schedule II or III in all settings (with physician documented approval); and prescribe and approve the use of durable medical equipment.

Physician assistants have prescriptive authority for therapeutic drugs and treatments within the scope of physician assistant practice, subject to biennial renewal. They may also prescribe medication for termination of pregnancy including Mifeprex, Mifepristone, and Misoprostol. Temporarily licensed PAs may not have a prescriptive practice.

A supervising physician may delegate to a fully licensed physician assistant authority to prescribe or dispense any medication used in the supervising physician's practice except those on a restricted formulary. Schedule II controlled substances limited to 7-day supply (14-day for Schedule II psychiatric mental health controlled substances for children under 18). General anesthetics and radiographic contrast materials prohibited. PA must complete 10 CE hours in specialty practice per renewal, including 3 hours on safe and effective prescribing of controlled substances.

Physician assistants may be delegated authority to issue prescription drug orders for dangerous drugs, Schedule III-V controlled substances, and (with at least 1 year post-licensure experience) hydrocodone/oxycodone in emergency situations (5-day limit, patients 18+). Cannot prescribe Schedule I or II controlled substances (except as noted above). Refills limited to 12 months from original order.

Physician assistants may prescribe controlled substances subject to supervision requirements; supervising physician must review at least 50% of controlled substance prescription records during first year of PA practice.

Physician assistants have prescriptive authority as determined by the board and the collaborative practice agreement; specific drug schedules not enumerated in the statute, but authority is set by board rules.

A collaborating physician may, but is not required to, delegate prescriptive authority to a physician assistant as part of a written collaborative agreement, conforming to the requirements of Section 7.5 of the Physician Assistant Practice Act of 1987.

A PA may prescribe and administer all nonscheduled legend drugs as delegated by the supervising physician. With board approval (after at least 1 year experience), a PA may prescribe Schedule III, IV, and V controlled substances as delegated by the supervising physician. Schedule III prescriptions limited to 30-day supply without refill; Schedule IV/V limited to 6-month supply total; benzodiazepines and Carisoprodol limited to 30-day supply without refill. PAs may not dispense controlled substances.

Physician associates may prescribe and dispense prescription and legend drugs including schedule II-V controlled substances as part of their scope of practice determined by practice setting. Dispensing (other than professional samples) is limited to situations where pharmacy service is not reasonably available, is in the patient's best interest, or an emergency exists.

A physician's assistant under a practice agreement may prescribe drugs, including controlled substances in schedules 2-5. PA's DEA registration number must be indicated on controlled substance prescriptions.

A physician assistant with a certificate of controlled substance prescriptive authority may prescribe Schedule III, IV, and V controlled substances and has restricted authority in Schedule II (limited to hydrocodone-containing medications), when delegated by a collaborative practice arrangement. Schedule III narcotic and Schedule II hydrocodone prescriptions limited to a 5-day supply without refill (except buprenorphine for MAT up to 30-day supply). Must register with the DEA and state bureau of narcotics.

Physician assistants are authorized to write prescriptions for drugs subject to Board regulations and supervising physician written instructions; must consult supervising physician before prescribing targeted controlled substances for pain management facilities or use exceeding 30 days.

A physician assistant may prescribe, dispense, administer, and procure drugs and medical devices; may prescribe and dispense schedule II through V substances and all legend drugs; may not dispense a drug unless pharmacy services are not reasonably available, dispensing is in the best interest of the patient, or an emergency exists; must register with DEA and comply with state and federal laws if prescribing controlled substances.

Physician assistants are approved to perform medical services under a collaborative agreement with the supervision of a physician; specific prescriptive authority scope is determined by rules and the collaborative agreement.

A physician assistant may order, prescribe, dispense, and administer medications and medical devices to the extent delegated by a supervising physician. Controlled dangerous substances (Schedules II-V) may only be ordered or prescribed if the supervising physician has authorized it and the PA has registered with the DEA and complied with all board requirements.
Physician assistants provide services with the supervision of or in collaboration with a licensed physician as set forth in rules promulgated by the board. The board establishes the scope by rule.

Physician assistants may prescribe controlled substances limited to the schedules of controlled substances that the supervising physician is authorized to prescribe under state and federal law. The Board and supervising physician shall limit such authority.
Physician assistants may prescribe within the scope defined by the practice agreement, which shall include the scope of and any limitations on prescribing

A physician associate is authorized to write prescriptions, including prescriptions for controlled substances listed in Schedules II through V. Physician associates may also register with the board for authority to dispense prescription drugs, but may not dispense controlled substances classified in Schedule I or II.

A physician assistant shall not independently prescribe or dispense drugs. The board shall promulgate regulations which permit a physician assistant to prescribe and dispense drugs at the direction of a physician.

PAs with permanent licenses may prescribe drug therapy as authorized in written scope of practice guidelines, including controlled substances in Schedules II-IV with restrictions. Schedule II oral controlled substances are limited to an initial 5-day supply; subsequent prescriptions require supervising physician consultation. Schedule II parenteral medications require hospital setting and specific oversight. PAs must maintain DEA registration and complete 4 CE hours every 2 years on controlled substance prescribing.

A physician may delegate prescribing of nonprescription drugs, dangerous drugs, and controlled substances in Schedules III-V (for up to 90 days per prescription). Schedule II controlled substances may only be delegated in hospital facility-based practice or for hospice patients. The combined number of APRNs and PAs to whom a physician may delegate prescriptive authority generally may not exceed seven (with exceptions for medically underserved populations and facility-based practices).

Associate physicians may prescribe Schedule III through V controlled substances if authorized under a collaborative practice arrangement and registered with the DEA mid-level practitioner registry; the collaborating physician must authorize specific controlled substances in the arrangement.

A licensed physician assistant has authority to prescribe controlled substances and devices as set forth in Chapter 34 as provided in a practice agreement or by credentialing and privileging requirements. Practice agreements must include a statement of controlled substances the PA is or is not authorized to prescribe.

Subject to board rules and consistent with experience, education, and training, a physician assistant may order, prescribe, procure, dispense, and administer prescription drugs, medical devices, services, and supplies.

A physician assistant may prescribe schedule II, III, IV, or V drugs. A physician assistant shall not prescribe schedule I drugs. A physician assistant may dispense prepackaged medications in rural clinics when pharmacy services are not physically available.

fields.rationale: Three distinct naming conventions appear: the common 'Board of Medical Examiners' pattern, a 'Medical Examining Board' variant, and a generic 'Review Panel' — each warrants its own bucket given the small distribution.

Said board shall (1) hear and decide matters concerning suspension or revocation of licensure, (2) adjudicate complaints against practitioners, and (3) impose sanctions where appropriate.
